title: How did our naughty bits get their names? | BODY ETYMOLOGY

entries.note: One of the Old English terms for the body.
From Old English bodig, of unknown origin further back; unusually it has no cognates in other Germanic languages, and in 'I found a body' it implies a corpse.
Like [[see:body]], an English word with no known cognate in related languages, discussed in an earlier episode.
Like [[see:body]], an English word whose history can't be traced back past a certain point.
Like [[see:body]], an English word with no known relatives in other Germanic languages.
The German word for body, from Latin [[from:corpus]].
Another German word for body, related to English [[same-root:life]].
Related to the German word for body, [[same-root:Leib]].
Rob's favourite Dutch word for body: the first part is related to [[same-root:lich]] and the second part means covering, so roughly the body frame.
An old word for body, now used mainly for a corpse; related to Dutch [[same-root:lichaam]] and to [[same-root:like]].
Mentioned as the meaning of [[see:lich]]; related to Latin [[from:corpus]].
In both of its senses it's related to [[same-root:lich]], probably through the idea of being shaped like something, since body and shape are linked ideas.
This adverb ending is related to [[same-root:like]] and [[same-root:lich]], and literally means like something.
Both the Dutch equivalent of the [[same-root:-ly]] ending and a Dutch word for body, the same thing as [[see:lichaam]].
From Greek [[from:anatomia]], dissection, literally a cutting up: ana means up or into pieces and the second root means to cut.
Shares the cutting root of [[same-root:anatomy]], and is often confused with etymology.
Jess believes it shares the cutting root of [[same-root:anatomy]], as a small piece of something.
From Old English heafod and related to Latin [[same-root:caput]] through a regular H/K consonant shift, so it is a cousin of [[same-root:capital]] and [[same-root:captain]].
One of the Latin-derived words related to [[same-root:head]], from Latin [[from:caput]].
Related to [[same-root:head]] despite having no consonant in common with it, because of the H/K sound shift.
Another Latin-derived relative of [[same-root:head]].
The hypothetical language spoken by all the Indo-European peoples, where the regular consonant shifts linking [[see:head]] and [[see:capital]] go back to.
Ultimately goes back to the same root as [[same-root:head]].
Related to [[same-root:hound]] through the same C/H shift that links [[see:head]] and [[see:capital]].
Related to [[same-root:canine]] through the C/H consonant shift.
Related to Latin [[same-root:centum]] through the C/H shift, as discussed in the numbers episode.
A Latin cognate of [[same-root:hundred]], given as another example of the C/H shift.
Old English brægen, possibly from a Greek word for the top of the skull; Anatoly Liberman's theories connect it to words for rubbish, rotten or broken.
An Old English word for the head that literally means brain locker.
An old word for the brain, easier for speakers of other Germanic languages to recognise because it resembles German [[same-root:Gehirn]].
The German word for brain, related to the Old English [[same-root:hernpan]].
The face is named as the part that faces someone, the thing people see, a logic shared by [[equivalent:visage]] and [[equivalent:Gesicht]].
Like [[same-root:face]], it means the part that can be seen, here of a building.
The French word for face, built on the verb to look, so basically the thing you can look at; compare [[equivalent:face]].
The German word for face, meaning a thing you look at, the same thought process as [[equivalent:visage]].
A very old word with relatives such as Dutch [[same-root:oog]], German [[same-root:Auge]] and Latin [[same-root:oculus]]; its root also appears in [[same-root:synopsis]] and [[same-root:myopic]].
The Dutch word for eye, not far from English [[same-root:eye]].
The German word for eye, a relative of [[same-root:eye]].
The Latin word for eye, showing that relatives of [[same-root:eye]] reach beyond the Germanic languages.
Another very old word for a part of the face.
Originally nosthyrl, from nose plus [[from:thrill]] in its old sense of a hole, so literally nose hole.
An old verb meaning to pierce or make a hole, found in [[gave:nostril]] and the Old English [[gave:eyethurl]].
Anglo-Saxon for window, literally an eye hole to glance through, used before English took the Danish-derived [[see:window]].
Taken from a Danish word meaning wind eye, and it replaced the Old English [[see:eyethurl]].
Related to [[same-root:eye]], it means seeing something together: syn- as in [[see:synergy]] plus -opsis, the looking part, so a whole plot in one summary.
Its syn- prefix is the same as the one in [[see:synopsis]].
Combines Latin [[from:ferus]], wild (related to [[same-root:feral]]), with a looking element, so ferocious means wild-looking.
Related to the first part of [[same-root:ferocity]], [[same-root:ferus]], wild.
Related to [[same-root:eye]]; it means having your eyes shut or a limited view.
Has always meant ear and comes from an ancient root meaning ear, shared with Latin [[same-root:auris]].
The Latin word for ear, which goes back to the same ancient word as [[same-root:ear]].
Originally meant a projection, probably the chin, rather than an opening.
Originally spelled tung; the -gue spelling was an overcorrection meant to guide pronunciation, and it makes the word look like French [[see:langue]].
The French word for tongue, whose -gue ending the English spelling of [[see:tongue]] may imitate.
Basically the same in Old English, except that it was spelled with a thorn.
The Old English name for the [[equivalent:Adam's apple]], where boll means a round seed pod, as in a cotton boll; a religiously neutral term.
Called the [[equivalent:throat boll]] in Old English, which Jess calls a religiously neutral alternative.
Made of Greek elements meaning to carry and to eat; its eating ending also appears in [[same-root:sarcophagus]].
Built on a similar idea to [[see:esophagus]] and related to [[same-root:gulp]].
Related to [[same-root:gullet]].
Means corpse-eater: the name first applied to a stone that made bodies seem to disappear, and it shares the eating ending of [[same-root:esophagus]].
Another word with the -phage eating element found in [[same-root:sarcophagus]].
Its root means something peeled off; the verb to skin came before the noun, and Old English used [[see:hide]] instead.
What Old English speakers called the body's covering before [[see:skin]].
From Greek skeleton soma, a dried-up body or mummy, meaning what is left after decay; also mentioned in the Halloween episode.
Resembles the Scandinavian words rather than West Germanic ones, which use their word for bone, as in [[see:Bein]], so it probably came from the Vikings.
Means both leg and bone in German, as in other West Germanic languages, which is why Rob says English [[see:leg]] should really be bone.
In Old English also the seat of soul, will, courage and intellect; through the C/H shift related to [[same-root:cardio]], [[same-root:courage]] and [[same-root:credible]].
Related to [[same-root:heart]] through the regular C/H consonant shift.
Related to [[same-root:heart]].
Related to [[same-root:heart]] and literally means being hearty, full of heart.
Related to [[same-root:heart]] through Latin [[from:credere]], to believe with all your heart.
Another relative of [[same-root:heart]] through Latin [[from:credere]].
Another relative of [[same-root:heart]] through Latin [[from:credere]].
Probably from an early Germanic root meaning not heavy, related to [[same-root:light]], perhaps because air-filled lungs float to the top of a stew pot.
In the sense of not heavy, related to [[same-root:lungs]].
Came from French in Middle English; its Latin and Greek predecessors referred to the throat, oesophagus, the whole digestive tract and even emotions.
Can mean any internal organ, one specific organ, or a beer belly, three uses in one word.
In Greek it meant the outer belly or paunch, but in English its descendants refer to internal gastric functions.
The Old English word for the stomach, and later the throat or gullet, was related to maw, which now usually means a mouth.
Probably a compound of Old English [[from?:cwiþ]], body, and a word for eggs, which makes kidneys body eggs.
An Old English word for body that is no longer used; probably the first element of [[gave?:kidney]].
Entered English in the 1300s from Latin [[from:botulus]], sausage; it briefly meant compassion, as in 'bowels of mercies' in the King James Colossians.
Related to [[same-root:bowels]] through Latin [[from:botulus]], sausage, and known for turning up in preserved foods.
Short for botulinum toxin, so related to [[same-root:botulism]].
From Middle English via Old French; it means insides and is related to [[same-root:internal]], not to trails, though folk etymology may have played a part.
Related to [[same-root:entrails]].
Also means internal, like [[see:entrails]].
Thought to be related to the Greek word for fat, like [[same-root:lipid]], perhaps because it looks greasy; probably unrelated to [[unrelated:live]].
Shares the Greek fat root with [[same-root:liver]].
Looks very like [[unrelated:liver]] but doesn't seem to be related to it.
German for liver, spelled almost like leben, to live, though the two don't seem to be related, mirroring English [[equivalent:liver]].
The intestine comes from a Greek word meaning food and is unrelated to the punctuation mark or [[unrelated:semicolon]]; the two Greek words converged in English.
Comes from a different Greek word from the intestinal [[unrelated:colon]].
Given alongside the punctuation colon when distinguishing it from the intestinal [[see:colon]].
Rob says his name means a column, in passing while separating the two kinds of [[see:colon]].
Discussed in an earlier episode.
Mixed up with [[see:colon]] in a recurring malapropism, 'I like the smell of your colon'.
Means something inflated, because toys, balloons, tools and sausages were often made from it.
Means entirely flesh or all raw flesh, from the prefix [[same-root:pan-]], all, plus a word for flesh, describing what it seemed to be made of.
A prefix meaning all or entire, found in [[see:pancreas]] and [[see:panacea]].
Contains the same prefix [[see:pan-]] as [[see:pancreas]].
Means straight, since that last bit of the intestine is straight, and it is related to [[same-root:erection]] and [[same-root:right]].
Related to [[same-root:rectum]].
Related to [[same-root:rectum]].
Literally just means ring.
Means a pitchfork, probably from the crook of the fork, with the legs as its tines.
From Old English [[from:grynde]], an abyss, depression or hollow between the legs; the spelling was probably influenced by [[see:loin]].
Probably influenced the spelling of [[see:groin]].
Most likely means a little hill, which also explains a town called Clitoris; Jess's Words from Hell entry opens with 'Congratulations, you found it.'
From Latin [[from:vagina]], so it means little vagina, i.e. little pod; covered in an earlier food episode.
In Latin a euphemism meaning pod or sheath, a place to park your sword, borrowed as the medical term; it gave [[gave:vanilla]].
The Anglo-Saxon 'c-word' was harmless in medieval times and means a sort of cleft; usage differs across the UK, US and Australia, with more saved for a swear-words episode.
In Latin it meant a tail as well as the male member, and it connects to [[same-root:pencil]] and [[same-root:penicillin]].
Related to [[same-root:penis]]; originally a word for a fine paintbrush.
Named for its paintbrush-like cells, so related to [[same-root:pencil]] and [[same-root:penis]].
An early English word for the penis, now more vulgar; originally a male bird that struts, like a rooster.
An early compound for the penis, from [[from:pill]], skin, plus [[from:cock]], so skin rooster; found in a 14th-century poem in the Kildare Lyrics about old age.
An Old English word for skin, related to [[same-root:peel]] and from an old word meaning to strip, as in [[same-root:pillage]].
Related to [[same-root:pill]], skin.
To strip someone of their possessions, from the same old word for stripping as [[same-root:pill]].
Also pudenda, a clinical term for the external genitals of either sex that literally means shame limb, like Old English [[equivalent:sceamlim]].
An Old English word with the same meaning as [[equivalent:pudendum]], showing how long people have felt ashamed of these parts.
Related to [[same-root:testify]], but the story of swearing oaths on testicles is groundless; more likely they bore witness to a child being male, like a [[same-root:testament]].
Discussed in the legal-terms episode; related to [[same-root:testicles]], though the oath-on-testicles story is a myth.
Testicles were a testament, or witness, that a child was male, which is the more likely link to [[same-root:testicles]].
The jokey German equivalent of balls, which Jess thinks fits 'body eggs' better than [[see:kidney]] does.
Earlier ballocks, simply meaning little balls.
The word means balls, i.e. testicles.
Thought to come from the Latin verb [[from:volvere]], to roll, like [[same-root:revolve]] and [[same-root:revolution]], since the outer genitals wrap around or enclose.
Related to [[same-root:vulva]].
Related to [[same-root:vulva]].
From an ancient root meaning joint, shared with the Greek word for angle in [[same-root:hexagon]]; the k was once pronounced, as in German [[same-root:Knie]].
Like [[see:knee]] and [[see:ankle]], it has a root meaning joint.
Also from a root meaning joint, and related to [[same-root:angle]].
Related to [[same-root:ankle]].
Contains the Greek word for angle, which shares a root with [[same-root:knee]].
Shares a root with [[same-root:knee]].
Shares a root with [[same-root:knee]].
Thought to come from an ancient root meaning five, the same root as the pent- in [[same-root:Pentagon]].
Its pent- is thought to share the root meaning five with [[same-root:finger]].
The Greek word for finger, seen in [[gave:pterodactyl]] (wing finger) and sharing a root with [[same-root:date]].
Means wing finger, from [[from:dactyl]].
The fruit shares a root with [[same-root:dactyl]]; it was sometimes called a finger fruit.
Rob thinks it just means swollen, so it is the fat finger.
The German word for knee, which still pronounces the k that [[same-root:knee]] once had.
Another German word for bones, which pleases Rob alongside [[see:Knie]] (knocking knees).
Linked to [[same-root:pedal]] and other Latin-derived words through regular F/P and D/T sound shifts; in Middle English it could also mean a person.
One of the Latin-derived relatives of [[same-root:foot]].
Related to [[same-root:tooth]] through the same D/T shift that links [[see:foot]] and [[see:pedal]].
Related to [[same-root:dental]] through regular consonant shifts.
A Middle English way of saying nobody, because [[see:foot]] could mean a person, much as sailors are called [[see:hands]].
Used for people on a boat, a comparison for [[see:foot]] meaning a person.
Thought to be related to words meaning to point or show, like [[same-root:indicate]], and perhaps somehow to [[same-root?:finger]]; some languages manage without a separate word.
Related to [[same-root:toe]] through a root meaning to point.
